growth_story.headline: Tourism lifted income per person in the Maldives to a record in 2025, but shocks make its growth among the most volatile anywhere, and debt is high
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2008 income per person grew 4.8 percent a year as the Maldives built a high-end resort economy, though the 2004 tsunami brought a fall of 12.6 percent in 2005 and a rebound of 20.7 percent in 2006. Growth slowed to 0.8 percent a year in 2009–2016: the global crisis cut tourism and income per person fell 11.5 percent in 2009, while the IMF described an unsustainable rise in public spending after the tsunami, dollar shortages and deep political division. From 2017 to 2025 growth picked up to 4.1 percent a year, carried by tourism and, until 2018, a public building programme paid for largely with foreign loans. The pandemic closed the borders in 2020 and income per person fell 34.8 percent, then rose 33.8 percent in 2021 and 12.1 percent in 2022. By 2025 income per person reached 12,499 in constant dollars, its highest level yet, but growth swings more than in almost any other economy (a standard deviation of 12.6 over 20 years), and the sources describe high public debt and strained foreign reserves left in part by the building of the past decade.

threads.title: One industry, many shocks
threads.text: Luxury tourism is the engine of the economy and has driven gains in living standards over three decades. The same reliance leaves the islands exposed to shocks from abroad. A larger airport terminal is expected to ease limits on tourist numbers.

threads.title: Tsunami, spending and the 2009 slump
threads.text: The 2004 tsunami brought the largest yearly drop in GDP on record: income per person fell 12.6 percent in 2005 before rising 20.7 percent in 2006. The IMF later described an unsustainable rise in public spending after the tsunami that the global crisis made worse, and income per person fell 11.5 percent in 2009. Deep political divisions then held back reform.

threads.title: A building boom on borrowed money
threads.text: A public building programme began in 2014, with projects such as the Sinamalé bridge, and construction became the other main driver of growth beside tourism. Investment reached 47.8 percent of GDP in 2018. The World Bank says the building of the past decade was paid for with foreign loans, alongside rising subsidies and a larger public wage bill.

threads.title: Pandemic collapse and rebound
threads.text: In 2020 the Maldives shut its borders to tourists for the first time, and income per person fell 34.8 percent, the deepest drop in the series. Tourism led the recovery once travel resumed: income per person rose 33.8 percent in 2021 and 12.1 percent in 2022, and passed its 2019 level in 2023.

since_last_year.text: In 2025 income per person grew 5.9 percent to its highest level, on strong tourist arrivals and a recovery in fishing. Since March 2026 the conflict in the Middle East has cut arrivals from Western markets, and reserves fell sharply in the first half of 2026 after a large sukuk bond was repaid. The World Bank's October 2026 note expects growth to slow in 2026 before picking up again in 2027.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes a public investment boom from 2014, and investment peaked at 47.8 percent of GDP in 2018, yet income per person grew only 4.3, 0.3, 2.7, 3.6 and 5.2 percent in 2014 to 2018. The boom also sits awkwardly with the eras: it began inside the 0.8 percent era, and growth in 2017–2025 (4.1 percent a year) stayed below the 1990–2008 pace. The World Bank's long-run story of rising living standards is told in current dollars; in constant prices the data show income per person a little more than doubling, from 5,580 in 1995 to 12,499 in 2025.
